shipped_rows.title_o: Is preview benefit from word n + 2 a common effect in reading Chinese? Evidence from eye movements

blind_target.authors: Yang, J., Wang, S., Xu, Y., & Rayner, K.
blind_target.title: Do chinese readers obtain preview benefit from word n+2? Evidence from eye movements.
blind_target.evidence_quote: In addition to investigating whether idioms are processed as single lexical units during reading, we also attempted to replicate the findings of Yang et al. (2009) and Yang et al. (2012) (i.e. word n+2 preview effects are only observed in Chinese text when word n+1 is highly frequent) in the same testing session as our main study.
blind_target.outcome_quote: This replication was successful, with us observing near identical effects to both Yang et al. studies when restricting our analysis to the same interest areas used in these studies.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly compare the tested finding with this original.

blind_target.authors: Cutter, M. G., Drieghe, D., & Liversedge, S. P.
blind_target.title: Preview benefit in English spaced compounds.
blind_target.evidence_quote: In the current study we investigated whether a similar phenomenon occurs in Chinese reading; namely, that when word n+2 forms a multi-word unit with word n+1, parafoveal processing of word n+2 may occur to a larger extent than previously observed.
blind_target.outcome_quote: It is worth considering the characteristics of our idioms which may have led to them not being processed as multi-word units in the parafovea, in contrast to the spaced compounds investigated by Cutter et al. (2014).
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly compare the tested finding with this original.

blind_target.authors: Underwood, G., Schmitt, N., & Galpin, A.
blind_target.title: The eyes have it: An eye-movement study into the processing of formulaic sequences.
blind_target.evidence_quote: First of all, the terminal word of our items received shorter fixations when they were part of an idiom as opposed to part of a phrase. This replicates an effect that has previously been observed in English idioms (see Underwood, Schmitt, & Galpin, 2004) and translated Chinese idioms (see Carrol & Conklin, 2015).

luna_triage.reason: Experiment 1 explicitly retests Yang et al. (2009) and reports its result as part of a successful replication. The only supplied shipped row is Yang et al. (2012), the separately cited follow-up whose title and DOI differ; the paper itself names both as distinct works, so that row does not represent the 2009 original.
luna_triage.location: Abstract; Experiment 1, introduction and discussion; References
luna_triage.omission_quote: We attempted to replicate these findings (Experiment 1)
luna_triage.identity_quote: Yang, J., Wang, S., Xu, Y., & Rayner, K. (2009). Do chinese readers obtain preview benefit from word n+2? Evidence from eye movements.
luna_triage.duplicate_quote: Yang, J., Rayner, K., Li., & Wang, S. (2012). Is preview benefit from word n+2 a common effect in reading Chinese? Evidence from eye movements.

luna_triage.reason: Experiment 2 tests whether the n+2 preview advantage reported for English spaced compounds also occurs when Chinese idiom constituents form a multiword unit. The paper reports the relevant preview and phrase-type effects and directly compares them with Cutter et al. (2014). No supplied row represents Cutter et al.

luna_triage.omission_quote: when word n+2 forms a multi-word unit with word n+1, parafoveal processing of word n+2 may occur to a larger extent than previously observed.
luna_triage.identity_quote: Cutter, M. G., Drieghe, D., & Liversedge, S. P. (2014). Preview benefit in English spaced compounds.

luna_triage.reason: Experiment 2 directly retests the reported shorter fixation time on the terminal word of idioms versus phrases and explicitly says this replicates the effect reported by Underwood et al. (2004). No supplied row represents that work.

This is an empirical retest in a different idiom set/context. No supplied row represents the cited work.
